new_elements: Vibration-done alert function (Uses haptic buzz instead of a bell or beep.)
rationale: Makes completion a physical sensation rather than a coded sound to interpret.
judge_comment: Haptic completion alert is simple and feasible, but it only helps if the user is touching the oven and it covers a minor part of operation.

title: 33 Wireless Power Pad
new_elements: Inductive power pad function (Replaces the mains cord connection with a fixed wireless power zone.)
rationale: Plug-in becomes place-the-oven-on-pad, simplifying setup.
judge_comment: Wireless power for a high-wattage microwave is inefficient and costly, and it barely affects the learning curve.

title: 34 Plasma Brown
new_elements: Microwave plasma browning function (A tiny low-current plasma path crisps surfaces without added oven modes.)
rationale: Solves a common disappointment automatically without teaching special settings.
judge_comment: Plasma browning is wildly novel and automatic, but it is dubious and unsafe inside a microwave cavity, and it doesn't substitute anything cheaper.

title: 35 Nucleation Strip
new_elements: Anti-superheat nucleation function (A cavity strip or cup liner seeds boiling so hot liquids do not erupt.)
rationale: Makes liquid heating safer without learned waiting and tapping rules.
judge_comment: A nucleation strip is concrete and plausible, and it removes the need to learn safety rules, though it is not core operation.

title: 36 RF-Safe Coating
new_elements: RF-safe cavity coating function (Coating and choke geometry tolerate small metal objects without arcing.)
rationale: Forgives common mistakes so the user does not need metal rules memorized.
judge_comment: Metal tolerance would remove a real rule users must learn, but safe arcing-free coating is technically doubtful and the mechanism is vague.

title: 37 Pulse-Count Timer
new_elements: RF pulse-count timer function (Timing is measured by magnetron pulses instead of a weak mechanical clock.)
rationale: Gives reliable short times so the user does not learn dial inaccuracies.
judge_comment: Counting magnetron pulses is a plausible timing substitute, but users never see it and it barely reduces the learning curve.

title: 38 Student Preset
new_elements: Student-mode preset function (Hides all settings and exposes only simple meals and one cancel.)
rationale: Directly serves the single-person household need by removing decision load.
judge_comment: A simplified mode is easy to build and clearly cuts decision load, but it is a common, unradical idea.

title: 39 Load Cell Time
new_elements: Load-cell cooking time function (Weighs the food and sets a safe automatic heating time.)
rationale: Turns portion judgment into a single place-and-start action.
judge_comment: Weighing the food to set the time gives place-and-start operation, and load cells are cheap and feasible, though weight alone is an imperfect proxy for heating needs.

title: 40 IR Thermal Window
new_elements: Infrared thermal window function (A thermal window shows hot zones instead of only visual cues.)
rationale: Makes doneness and danger more intuitive than checking by sight alone.
judge_comment: A thermal view helps judge doneness intuitively, but it adds information to interpret rather than simplifying operation, and a window through the shielding is hard to build.

title: 41 Rotating Housing
new_elements: Rotating housing cavity function (Rotates the whole food-side cavity instead of using a tray motor.)
rationale: Removes small tray alignment and cleaning steps.
judge_comment: Rotating the whole cavity is radical but mechanically complex and only marginally helps learning-free operation.

title: 42 Capacitive Door Strip
new_elements: Capacitive door-open strip function (A long touch strip opens the door instead of a small button.)
rationale: Leverages natural grasp instead of locating a hidden push button.
judge_comment: A large touch strip for opening the door directly removes a hunt-for-the-button friction and is readily buildable.

title: 43 Foam Choke
new_elements: RF foam choke function (Replaces precision metal rim sealing with compliant foam-based RF control.)
rationale: Door closure becomes more forgiving and easier for novices.
judge_comment: Foam RF choke is a named mechanism but the user benefit is indirect and RF leakage safety is a concern.

title: 44 GaN RF Source
new_elements: GaN RF source function (Uses semiconductor RF generation instead of the classic high-voltage diode path.)
rationale: Can hide complex electrical behavior behind simpler on-off operation.
judge_comment: Solid-state GaN RF is real and emerging, but it barely changes the user's operating experience.

title: 45 Software Watchdog
new_elements: Software interlock watchdog function (One safety sensor is supervised by firmware instead of three mechanical switches.)
rationale: Simplifies door mechanics and reduces learned failure symptoms.
judge_comment: Replacing redundant mechanical interlocks with firmware supervision is regulatory-risky and invisible to the user.

title: 46 Voice Recipe
new_elements: Voice recipe controller function (Says reheat soup or defrost bread and confirms with one button.)
rationale: Replaces abstract settings with ordinary language and confirmation.
judge_comment: Voice commands in plain language with a confirm button simplify operation, but voice-controlled microwaves already exist and it adds components rather than substituting cheaper ones.

title: 47 Three-Meal Button
new_elements: One-button three meals function (One button cycles through only soup, rice, and plate presets.)
rationale: Reduces option overload to a tiny learnable set.
judge_comment: A single button cycling three presets is simple and cheap to build, but it is an obvious reduction and limits flexibility.

title: 48 Self-Wiping Tray
new_elements: Self-wiping rotating tray function (Uses an edge blade and rotation to keep the tray clean during heating.)
rationale: Automatically maintains a visible core part so users need no cleanup ritual.
judge_comment: A self-wiping tray is imaginative, but it targets cleaning rather than operation, and a blade in a microwave is impractical and unsafe.

title: 49 Bellless Door
new_elements: Bellless door closure function (Uses latch resistance and a done light instead of a mechanical bell.)
rationale: Removes an old-world signal that many beginners misread.
judge_comment: Replacing the bell with a done light is easy and a little relevant, but it is a minor change that may reduce usability for people who rely on sound.

title: 50 No-Knob Microwave
new_elements: Knobless one-action function (The whole operation is put food in and close door.)
rationale: Achieves the purest zero-learning form of microwave operation.
judge_comment: Close-the-door-and-go is the ideal zero-learning concept, but it does not say how the microwave knows the food type or heating time, so it is underspecified and risks poor results.

title: One-Button Start
new_elements: One-Button Start Interface (Single physical button replaces all microwave controls.); OnePressCook (One press starts a safe default cooking cycle.); Full Control Panel (Timer, power, menu, and start controls.)
rationale: It removes all settings so users need learn only one press.
judge_comment: Highly relevant and very feasible, but a single-button microwave is a fairly obvious simplification and not radical.

title: Pull-Cord Start
new_elements: Pull-Cord Start Handle (A pull cord replaces push buttons and knobs.); PullToStart (Pulling starts a fixed short heating cycle.); Electronic Control Buttons (Physical push buttons and rotary selectors.)
rationale: Pulling is instinctive and avoids menu learning.
judge_comment: The pull cord is quirky and intuitive, but it adds wear and safety concerns and offers little advantage over a button.

title: Squeeze Handle Start
new_elements: Door Squeeze Trigger (Squeezing the door handle starts heating.); GripStart (One natural grip action starts cooking.); Door Release Button (Separate push-release button.)
rationale: Users start without locating buttons.
judge_comment: Squeezing the handle is a natural gesture that merges door and start, though accidental starts and the safety interlock complicate it.

title: Foot-Plate Start
new_elements: Foot-Plate Start (Stepping on a base plate starts cooking.); FootStart (Hands-free start for carrying food.); Top Panel Start Button (Control-panel button.)
rationale: It removes panel interaction entirely.
judge_comment: The foot plate is unusual and hands-free, but it is awkward, a safety risk, and not obviously simpler to learn.

title: Voice Phrase Start
new_elements: Voice Phrase Button (Speaking start replaces pressing controls.); SayToStart (Natural voice command starts fixed default cycle.); Control Panel Interface (Manual buttons and dials.)
rationale: It lets users start without learning icons.
judge_comment: Voice start needs no learning in principle, but noisy kitchens, accents and the vague mechanism limit it, and voice control is already common.

title: Barcode Scan Start
new_elements: Barcode Scanner (Scan food package replaces manual settings.); BarcodeAutoCook (Scan sets time and power automatically.); Timer and Power Knobs (Manual cooking selectors.)
rationale: No learning curve because the package tells the machine.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning sets cook parameters automatically, which is useful but already exists in some products, and it works only for packaged food.

title: RFID Preset Tray
new_elements: RFID Food Tray (Tray tags replace knobs.); TagAutoCook (Tray identifies food and runs preset.); Preset Button Row (Food preset buttons.)
rationale: Users just place food on a self-programming surface.
judge_comment: Tag-based identification of food is workable but requires tagged trays or food, and keeping preset buttons undermines the simplicity.

title: QR Code Start
new_elements: QR Code Camera (Camera scans QR labels replacing controls.); QRAutoCycle (Scanned code launches preset.); Display Menu (On-device menu system.)
rationale: Simple scanning avoids interface comprehension.
judge_comment: QR scanning is nearly the same as the barcode idea and keeps a menu display, so it adds complexity.

title: Weight Trigger Auto-Cycle
new_elements: Weight Sensor Plate (Sensor starts when item placed.); PlaceToCook (Weight triggers fixed cook cycle.); Timer Knob (Manual duration selector.)
rationale: Users need not set time because the load decides.
judge_comment: Placing the item to start is simple, but weight alone says little about the right cook time, and the retained timer knob still requires learning.

title: Steam-Cutoff Stop
new_elements: Steam Sensor (Sensor replaces user monitoring.); AutoDone (Steam pattern stops heating when done.); User Stop Button (Manual stop control.)
rationale: It removes learning about stopping times.
judge_comment: Steam sensing to detect doneness is proven in sensor-cook microwaves and removes guesswork, though it is not very radical.

title: Turntable Dial Start
new_elements: Turntable Set Dial (Rotating turntable edge sets time.); SpinToCook (Spin to select and start.); Timer Knob (Front timer control.)
rationale: It uses a visible moving part as a simple dial.
judge_comment: Spinning the turntable rim to set time and start is intuitive and substitutes a dial for the keypad, though sensing rotation under load and wet or hot conditions is tricky.

title: Door-Close Auto Start
new_elements: Auto Start After Preset (Closing door starts after simple dial set.); CloseToStart (Door closing activates selected preset.); Start Button (Separate start control.)
rationale: It eliminates an extra button step.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start is simple and feasible, but it is a known pattern and still keeps a separate start button, which weakens the substitution.

title: Color Coded Food Dial
new_elements: Color Food Dial (Colored food icons replace numbers.); ColorPresetSelect (Turn to color starts preset.); Numeric Timer Scale (Minutes-based dial.)
rationale: Color matching is easier than reading time.
judge_comment: Colored food icons are easy to understand and cheap to build, but the idea is incremental and the numeric scale remains.

title: Single Detent Preset Dial
new_elements: Detent Preset Dial (Few mechanical detents replace many buttons.); DetentOneShot (Lift detent starts one preset.); Preset Button Matrix (Array of menu buttons.)
rationale: One lift action is discoverable and avoids menus.
judge_comment: A few mechanical detents with a lift-to-start action cut menu complexity, but the lift gesture is not obvious without learning.

title: Linear Slider Power
new_elements: Linear Power Slider (Slider replaces 5-step power knob.); SlidePower (Move slider once to adjust intensity.); Power Knob Cam (Rotary cam power selector.)
rationale: Linear motion is easier than rotational power coding.
judge_comment: A slider is a plausible, cheap swap for the power knob, but it only addresses one control and adds little to the overall learning curve.

title: Touchless Hover Dial
new_elements: Hover Gesture Dial (Hand hovering over ring adjusts presets.); HoverPreset (Wave to choose and start.); Capacitive Buttons (Touch buttons requiring presses.)
rationale: It avoids cleaning and precise button presses.
judge_comment: A hover-gesture dial with wave-to-start is intuitive in concept, but gestures need discovering and can trigger accidentally, so it only partly removes the learning curve.

title: Transparent Door
new_elements: Fully Transparent Door (Clear casing replaces lamp and door holes.); DirectInsideView (See food without internal lighting.); Interior Lamp and Perforations (Light and viewing holes.)
rationale: No need to understand door holes and lighting.
judge_comment: A fully transparent door is not feasible because the microwave shielding mesh is needed, and it does little for operation simplicity.

title: Internal Webcam
new_elements: Internal Webcam (Camera replaces internal lamp for visibility.); AppedLiveView (User sees contents remotely without opening.); Door Viewing Holes (Hole-based door window.)
rationale: Simple external viewing avoids guesswork.
judge_comment: A webcam with an app is workable, but the app adds complexity, which works against the no-learning-curve goal.

title: External Status Light
new_elements: Status Light Halo (One colored halo replaces display and lamp.); ColorProgress (Halo shows start, heating, done.); Numeric Display (Screen showing time.)
rationale: One light is easier to read than a screen.
judge_comment: One color halo for start, heating and done is simple, cheap and easy to build, and it cuts the reading effort.

title: No Lamp Auto Done
new_elements: Thermal Done Sensor (Thermal sensor replaces internal lamp and checking.); NoLampAutoDone (Cavity senses done without visible light.); Interior Incandescent Lamp (Old lamp inside cavity.)
rationale: It removes the need to observe cooking.
judge_comment: Sensing doneness automatically removes the need to set times or watch the food, which directly serves effortless use, though reliable thermal sensing inside a microwave is hard.

title: Pop-Up Food Rack
new_elements: Pop-Up Food Rack (Rack lifts food replacing door release.); PushToPresent (Press door and rack presents food.); Door Push-Release Button (Manual release mechanism.)
rationale: Opening becomes automatic and easy.
judge_comment: Automatic food presentation is a fun twist, but it only affects opening the door and does little for the learning curve of operating the cooking controls.

title: Fixed Power Simple Time
new_elements: Fixed-Power Time Dial (One dial replaces power and timer knobs.); TimeOnlyCook (Set minutes, fixed wattage cook.); Five-Step Power Knob (Power selector.)
rationale: Fewer controls leave one task for the user.
judge_comment: A single time dial is simple and highly feasible, but it is a well-known approach and not radical.

title: Mechanical Tick Stop
new_elements: Clockwork Tick Dial (Audible dial replaces digital display.); TickToDone (User hears time and stop bell.); Electronic Display (Digital timer.)
rationale: Familiar clock sound reduces learning.
judge_comment: A mechanical clockwork dial is familiar and intuitive and cheap, but it already exists in older microwaves.

title: Auto-Power Mass
new_elements: Mass-Based Power Control (Sensor sets power replacing user knob.); AutoWattage (Power chosen from load mass.); Power Knob (Manual wattage selector.)
rationale: Users choose nothing beyond placing food.
judge_comment: Auto power chosen from load mass removes a decision, but mass alone is a poor proxy for how food should be cooked, so it may be unreliable.

title: Food Label Time
new_elements: Optical Label Reader (Reader sees label color and size and sets time.); LabelTime (Time inferred from visible food cue.); Timer Knob (Manual duration knob.)
rationale: The label guides cooking so the user learns nothing.
judge_comment: Inferring cook time from a label or visual cue with an optical reader is radical and removes all input, but reliability is doubtful and the reader adds cost.

title: Static Cavity
new_elements: Static Food Shelf (Fixed shelf replaces turntable motor.); StillCook (Food stays in simple position.); Glass Turntable and Motor (Rotating base.)
rationale: Fewer moving parts reduce confusion and failure.
judge_comment: Removing the turntable is a simple substitution but barely affects operational simplicity, and uneven heating is a downside; it's also not radical.

title: Handle-Twist Timer
new_elements: Handle-Twist Dial (Twisting door handle sets and starts time.); TwistDoorCook (One handle motion selects duration.); Front Timer Knob (Separate timer dial.)
rationale: It uses door interaction as the main control.
judge_comment: Twisting the door handle to set and start the time is intuitive and unusual, and it is mechanically plausible.

title: One Button Preset Cycle
new_elements: Preset Cycle Button (Button steps through presets on press.); ButtonCycle (Short press cycles, long press starts.); Preset Buttons (Multiple food buttons.)
rationale: One control can be learned instead of many buttons.
judge_comment: A single cycling button reduces the number of controls, but cycling through presets with short and long presses introduces a hidden learning curve.

title: Preprogrammed Food Mat
new_elements: Silicone Preset Mat (Embedded NFC mat replaces buttons.); MatPreset (Mat sets time and power.); Preset Button Panel (Front food presets.)
rationale: Food item itself selects the program.
judge_comment: An NFC mat that selects the program from the food placed on it is intuitive, and the technology is feasible, but it requires a specific mat for each food.

title: Food Brick RFID
new_elements: RFID Food Brick (Tagged brick on shelf replaces knobs.); BrickProgram (Brick identifies food to start.); Manual Control Cluster (Timer and power controls.)
rationale: Users insert a tag instead of learning settings.
judge_comment: RFID tags that identify the food avoid settings, but users must manage and keep track of bricks, and the manual controls still remain.

title: Food-Shaped Button
new_elements: Popcorn-Shaped Button (Real-food icon buttons replace menu text.); IconStart (Press shape to start common task.); Text Menu (Labelled control panel.)
rationale: Icon shapes are easier than reading text.
judge_comment: Real-food icon buttons are intuitive and easy to build, but they are fairly incremental and already resemble existing preset buttons.

title: No-Screen Voice
new_elements: Speaker-Mic Ring (Speaker and mic replace screen.); VoiceOnePhrase (One spoken phrase starts default.); Control Display (Visual panel.)
rationale: Talking is easier than reading a panel.
judge_comment: A one-phrase voice start is simple and feasible, though voice microwaves already exist and noisy kitchens or accents can cause problems.

title: Color Finish Light
new_elements: Color-Changing Skin (Whole casing changes color when done.); SkinDone (Color shift replaces timer reading.); Numeric Display (Time display.)
rationale: A big visible change is simple to interpret.
judge_comment: A color-changing casing is eye-catching and easy to read, but it only signals completion and not how to operate the microwave, and the tech is costly.

title: Sound Cues Instead of Display
new_elements: Audio Cue Chimes (Different tones replace screen information.); SoundProgress (Chimes indicate start, heating, done.); Timer Screen (Visual display.)
rationale: Listening is lower learning than reading.
judge_comment: Audio chimes are cheap and feasible but common, and they do not help with setting up the operation.

title: Haptic Dial Without Labels
new_elements: Haptic Time Knob (Clicks and vibration replace numbers.); FeelPreset (User feels detents and stops.); Printed Scale (Visual numeric scale.)
rationale: Tactile detents can be learned by touch.
judge_comment: A haptic detent knob without labels is plausible and tactile, but removing the numbers may actually raise the learning curve for new users.

title: Start by Loading Item
new_elements: Load Plate Switch (Plate under turntable starts fixed cycle.); PlaceToStart (Item placement triggers start.); Start Button (Manual start control.)
rationale: Cooking starts automatically when food is loaded.
judge_comment: A load-sensing plate that auto-starts a fixed cycle removes the start step, but it risks accidental starts and gives no control over cooking time.

title: Door Open Auto Stop
new_elements: Door Interlock Auto Stop (Opening door stops heating.); OpenStop (User does not press stop.); Stop Button (Manual stop control.)
rationale: The common stop action is simply opening the door.
judge_comment: Opening the door already stops heating on every microwave, so this is not new and barely reduces learning.

title: Auto Thermal Stop
new_elements: Auto Thermal Stop (Thermal cut-out replaces manual stopping.); ThermalCutoff (Heating stops at safe temperature.); User Stop Control (Stop button.)
rationale: No need to know stop timing.
judge_comment: A thermal cut-out removes the need to judge timing, but food temperature is hard to sense and a cut-out is a safety device, not a cooking control.

title: Time-Only Knob
new_elements: Time-Only Knob (One knob removes power selection.); MinuteOnly (Turn to minutes and go.); Two Knob Interface (Power plus time controls.)
rationale: One task is all the user must learn.
judge_comment: A single minutes knob is very simple and cheap, but similar designs already exist and it gives up power control.

title: Handle Start Unlock
new_elements: Handle-Integrated Start (Pulling handle starts and unlocks.); PullCookStop (Pull starts, second pull stops.); Push-Release Button (Door button.)
rationale: Door handling becomes the operation.
judge_comment: Using the handle pull to start and stop is an intuitive substitution, but the door-opening logic conflicts with loading food and the mechanism is unclear.

title: Magnetic Key Start
new_elements: Magnetic Key Panel (Physical key replaces buttons.); KeyTurnCook (Insert and turn starts preset.); Digital Control Board (Complex electronics panel.)
rationale: A mechanical key is intuitive and cheap.
judge_comment: A key start is simple, but a key can be lost and it doesn't say what to cook or for how long; it's modestly novel.

title: Phone Tap Start
new_elements: Phone Tap Start (Tap-to-start phone replaces panel.); NFCPhoneStart (Tap phone to start default.); Built-In Buttons (Microwave control buttons.)
rationale: A familiar phone action removes learning.
judge_comment: NFC tap is feasible but requires a phone and a default program, so it adds friction for a no-learning-curve goal.

title: Watch Tap Start
new_elements: Watch Tap Start (Smartwatch tap replaces button.); WristStart (Raise wrist and tap to start.); Front Control Panel (Built-in panel.)
rationale: Wearable tap is simple and direct.
judge_comment: It needs a smartwatch, which is even less universal than a phone and mostly a variant of idea 2.

title: Lever Start Stop
new_elements: Push-Pull Lever (Lever replaces start and stop buttons.); LeverCook (Push to start, pull to stop.); Dual Button Panel (Start and stop buttons.)
rationale: One mechanical action replaces two buttons.
judge_comment: A push-pull lever is intuitive and cheap, but it handles only start/stop and not time or power.

title: Pre-Baked Time Dial
new_elements: Common Food Dial (Dial shows only water, popcorn, pizza icons.); FoodIconTime (Turn icon and start.); 30-Minute Timer (Fine minute scale.)
rationale: It removes the need to know minutes.
judge_comment: A food-icon dial directly removes the need to know cooking times, is cheap and easy to build, and is the best fit for the need.

title: LED Remaining Ring
new_elements: Remaining LED Ring (Ring shrinks as time passes.); VisualCountdown (One ring replaces numeric clock.); Digital Display (Digits screen.)
rationale: Ring length is easier to interpret than time.
judge_comment: A shrinking LED ring is simple to build and intuitive to read, but it only changes the countdown display and does not simplify input.

title: No Clock Removal
new_elements: Clock-Free Interface (No wall clock setting.); NoClockCook (Only cooking function remains.); Clock Setting Controls (Clock adjustment buttons.)
rationale: Removing clock setup simplifies operation.
judge_comment: Dropping clock setup removes a real friction point and is easy to do, but it is an incremental change rather than a radical one.

title: Unlock Knob Timer
new_elements: Unlock Timer Knob (Turning knob unlocks door and sets time.); UnlockStart (One motion prepares cooking.); Door Button and Timer (Separate controls.)
rationale: It integrates door access with start.
judge_comment: A single knob turn that opens the door and sets the time is intuitive and mechanically plausible, though how the door unlocks is unclear.

title: Whole Door Capacitive Start
new_elements: Door Surface Sensor (Anywhere door touch starts preset.); TouchDoorStart (Touch door to cook.); Button Panel (Dedicated buttons.)
rationale: Large surface is easier than small buttons.
judge_comment: A large touch surface is easy to hit, but accidental starts are a safety risk and a preset gives little control.

title: Closing Door Default Cook
new_elements: Closing Door Default Cook (Closing door starts one default short cycle.); CloseDefaultCook (No settings for basic warming.); Timer and Start Buttons (Manual start controls.)
rationale: Users only close the door for basic use.
judge_comment: Starting on door close removes all learning, but it risks heating an empty cavity or starting unintentionally, which makes it a safety problem.

title: I01 One-Twist Color Timer
new_elements: I01 Color-ring twist timer (A twist dial whose only cue is a colored band that shortens as the wait time is set)
rationale: A single color twist replaces numbers and marks, so first-time users can choose a wait without learning the scale.
judge_comment: A color band with no numbers is intuitive in concept, but users may not know what duration a color maps to, so it may not remove the learning curve.

title: I02 One-Press Timed Cycle
new_elements: I02 One-press timed cycle (A single big button starts a safe preset cycle for a typical mug or plate)
rationale: One press gives a predictable default, removing the need to set minutes at all.
judge_comment: One button with a preset cycle is the simplest possible operation and easy to build, but it is not novel and a single preset suits few foods.

title: I03 Wind-Up Spring Timer
new_elements: I03 Wind-up spring timer (A spring-wound dial counts down and trips a mechanical stop when empty, like a kitchen timer)
rationale: The familiar wind-and-release motion needs no explanation and avoids mains-frequency motor timing complexity.
judge_comment: Mechanical wind-up timers are familiar and proven in old microwaves, so they work well but are barely new.

title: I04 Sandglass Visual Timer
new_elements: I04 Sandglass visual timer (A sealed sandglass on the fascia shows remaining time by visible falling grains)
rationale: A universal time symbol gives immediate feedback without reading a digital clock or dial.
judge_comment: A sandglass gives nice feedback, but it is fixed-duration, can't be set, and is awkward to reset, so it does little to simplify operation.

title: I05 Door-As-Knob Timer
new_elements: I05 Door-as-knob timer (The door handle itself is a mechanical timer: pull it out to set time, release to start)
rationale: Pulling the door naturally encodes duration and operation into one gesture, eliminating separate timer settings.
judge_comment: Combining the door and timer into one gesture is radical and intuitive, but the mechanics and safety interlocks make it hard to build.

title: I06 Food-Weight Auto-Stop
new_elements: I06 Food-weight auto-stop (A weighted plate starts a fixed cycle as soon as food is placed)
rationale: Weight replaces settings: put food in, and the appliance chooses a safe standard time.
judge_comment: A weighted plate that starts a fixed cycle removes settings entirely, but weight alone is a poor proxy for heating time and starting automatically raises safety concerns.

title: I07 Single Warm/Hot Button
new_elements: I07 Single warm hot button (Two large buttons labeled warm and hot replace the five-step power dial)
rationale: A binary choice is easier than a multi-level power scale and needs no explanation.
judge_comment: Two labeled buttons are very easy to use and trivially buildable, but this is an incremental simplification rather than a radical idea.

title: I08 Defrost Without a Dial
new_elements: I08 One-pat defrost pad (A soft pad on the door initiates a safe low-duty defrost cycle when tapped)
rationale: One pat replaces a power level and defrost program, so users need not understand low-power cycling.
judge_comment: A single pat pad for defrost is intuitive and feasible, though a door-mounted soft pad and accidental triggering are concerns.

title: I09 Auto-Melt Trigger
new_elements: I09 Auto melt trigger (A fixed gentle melt cycle starts by pressing a large melt icon once)
rationale: A single obvious task button removes all power-level guessing for butter or chocolate.
judge_comment: A single melt button is simple and easy to implement, but it is a narrow preset and not very novel.

title: I10 Color-Food Preset Slots
new_elements: I10 Color food preset slots (Molded colored food-shape slots in the fascia set time and power by the shape placed in them)
rationale: Physical food shapes make setting time and power self-evident rather than abstract.
judge_comment: Physical food-shape slots that set time and power make settings tangible and are fairly novel, but the mechanism is vague and food variety is limited.

title: I11 Pull Chain Time-Off Timer
new_elements: I11 Pull chain time off timer (A pull chain sets a simple countdown; another pull stops early, like a lamp cord)
rationale: A familiar pull action replaces rotating knob settings and provides an obvious way to interrupt.
judge_comment: A pull-chain timer is familiar and intuitive for start and stop, and it substitutes cheaply for a knob, though pull-count-to-time mapping is vague.

title: I12 Foot-Pedal Door Release
new_elements: I12 Foot-pedal door release (A soft floor pedal opens the door when hands are loaded with food or dishes)
rationale: A natural foot action makes door opening simpler when hands are busy, with no buttons to find.
judge_comment: A foot pedal helps when hands are full and is mechanically simple, but it only addresses door opening and adds a floor item.

title: I13 One-Hand Strap Door
new_elements: I13 One-hand strap door (A soft pull strap opens the door by instinctive pulling instead of pressing a release button)
rationale: Pulling is easier than locating and pressing a small button, so users need no explanation.
judge_comment: A pull strap or handle is intuitive and cheap, but it is close to existing handle-pull doors and not very radical.

title: I14 Auto-Pop Door at End
new_elements: I14 Auto-pop door at end (A spring latch pops the door open when cooking ends, replacing interpretation of the bell)
rationale: The door opening itself communicates completion, so no separate sound or button action is needed.
judge_comment: Auto-popping the door at the end clearly signals completion and removes a step, and spring-latch doors already exist in microwaves.

title: I15 Magnetic Handle-Free Door
new_elements: I15 Magnetic handle-free door (A large magnetic patch unlatches the door with a single hand tap)
rationale: A big obvious tap area removes tiny-button fumbling and makes opening almost reflexive.
judge_comment: A magnetic tap-to-release door is easy to use, but the mechanism is vague and risks accidental opening or safety-interlock issues.

title: I16 Fully Transparent Cavity
new_elements: I16 Fully transparent cavity (A microwave-reflective visible-transparent enclosure replaces perforated door and interior lamp)
rationale: Users see everything without needing to learn about light, mesh, or viewing windows.
judge_comment: A transparent conductive enclosure is plausible, since existing mesh doors already do this, but it mainly improves visibility and does little for operating simplicity.

title: I17 Glow-in-the-Dark Walls
new_elements: I17 Glow-in-the-dark cooking walls (A heat-reactive phosphor lining illuminates the cavity during use, eliminating a bulb)
rationale: Automatic glow gives visibility without the user switching on a light or replacing a burnt-out lamp.
judge_comment: Heat-reactive phosphor lighting is novel, but phosphors would glow dimly and unreliably in a cavity, and it does little for the no-learning-curve need.

title: I18 Heat-Stripe Countdown
new_elements: I18 Heat-stripe countdown (External heat-sensitive stripes darken in order to show remaining cooking time)
rationale: A changing color strip is an intuitive countdown that needs no reading of numbers or waiting for a ding.
judge_comment: A thermochromic countdown stripe is intuitive and needs no reading, though making it reversible and accurate over time is difficult.

title: I19 Steam-Stop Visual Alert
new_elements: I19 Steam-stop visual alert (A steam-sensitive patch flashes when heating is complete, replacing the mechanical bell)
rationale: A visible signal tied to food condition is easier to notice than a bell that may be hidden by noise.
judge_comment: A visual end-of-cooking alert is useful, but a steam-sensitive patch that flashes is technically vague and unreliable.

title: I20 Scent Bell
new_elements: I20 Scent bell (A tiny scent capsule releases a pleasant aroma at end of cooking to replace the ding)
rationale: A smell cannot be mistaken for noise from another appliance and gives a simple end signal without buttons.
judge_comment: A scent signal is highly radical and unmistakable, but it needs consumable capsules, is slow to register, and is hard to control.

title: I21 Haptic End-of-Cooking Pulse
new_elements: I21 Haptic end pulse (The door edge gives one soft vibration pulse when cooking ends)
rationale: A single pulse is an unmistakable touch signal, easier to understand than a bell or visual alert.
judge_comment: A haptic pulse is plausible but only marginally helps ease of operation, and it doesn't substitute a part in a meaningful way.

title: I22 Turntableless Wave Floor
new_elements: I22 Turntableless wave floor (A molded ceramic floor shapes the field so food heats evenly without a rotating tray)
rationale: No tray to place or rotate means users do not need to learn microwave positioning rules.
judge_comment: Removing the turntable simplifies use, and stirrer or shaped-floor designs exist, but a ceramic floor alone is unlikely to give truly even heating.

title: I23 Air-Driven Plate
new_elements: I23 Air-driven plate (Cooling airflow pushes a lightweight plate in a slow orbit, removing the turntable motor)
rationale: A passive spinning surface gives even heating without the user noticing the mechanism.
judge_comment: Airflow-driven rotation is creative and replaces the motor, but a fan's airflow is unlikely to turn a loaded plate reliably, and there's heat and grease to contend with.

title: I24 RF-Pressure Spin Plate
new_elements: I24 RF-pressure spin plate (A lightweight disk is slowly pushed by asymmetric RF pressure without gears or motors)
rationale: Self-rotating heating needs no setup and hides the complexity from the user entirely.
judge_comment: Radiation pressure from microwaves is far too tiny to rotate a plate with food, so this is physically implausible, though very radical.

title: I25 Bowl-Shaped Cavity
new_elements: I25 Bowl-shaped cavity (Curved cavity walls focus and spread fields so plates heat evenly without being rotated)
rationale: Geometry performs the equalization job, so users no longer need to center food on a turntable.
judge_comment: Curved walls could reduce the need for centering, but cavity geometry alone can't reliably equalize fields across varied loads.

title: I26 No-Roller Ceramic Ball Plate
new_elements: I26 No-roller ceramic ball plate (The plate rests on a ceramic ball and rotates with any gentle plate movement)
rationale: A familiar plate and ball mechanism is easier to use than a motorized tray with rollers.
judge_comment: A ball-supported plate that rotates with gentle movement is plausible, but it does little for the no-learning-curve need and a passive plate would not rotate on its own.

title: I27 Stirrer Window Instead of Turntable
new_elements: I27 Stirrer-window waveguide (A rotating antenna window distributes fields so food need not move on a turntable)
rationale: The user can simply place food anywhere, because distribution is done by the field itself.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in real microwaves, so this is highly feasible and removes the turntable, though it is not very radical.

title: I28 Passive Thermal Rotator
new_elements: I28 Passive thermal rotator (Warm air currents in a sealed cushion rotate the plate without a motor)
rationale: The plate turns by itself, so there is nothing for the user to assemble or remember.
judge_comment: Using warm air in a sealed cushion to turn a plate is imaginative but physically implausible and would deliver unreliable torque.

title: I29 Molded Energy-Diffuser Shelf
new_elements: I29 Molded energy-diffuser shelf (A fixed shaped shelf creates many mild hot spots that average out over the plate)
rationale: A simple shelf removes turntable setup while keeping even-heating results familiar.
judge_comment: A fixed shelf that shapes the field is conceivable, but averaging hot spots without movement is unlikely to heat evenly.

title: I30 Iconless Molded Control Shapes
new_elements: I30 Iconless molded control shapes (Physical bumps and grooves stand in for words, numbers, and icons on the fascia)
rationale: Tactile shapes make operation obvious without needing labels, numbers, or symbols.
judge_comment: Tactile control shapes make the interface more intuitive and are easy to mold, though removing all numbers and labels could hurt clarity for setting times.

title: I31 Close-Door Auto Start
new_elements: I31 Close-door auto start (Closing the door starts a safe short default cycle without any knob or button press)
rationale: The most natural action, closing the door, becomes the start command, so there is literally nothing to set.
judge_comment: Closing the door as the start command removes every control, though accidental starts and empty-cavity runs need safeguards, and it is not very radical.

title: I32 Insert-and-Glow Start
new_elements: I32 Insert-and-glow start (Placing food on a weighted mat starts a fixed cycle and makes the cavity glow to confirm it)
rationale: Weight and glow combine into a single intuitive signal that cooking has begun without controls.
judge_comment: A weighted mat that starts the cycle is intuitive, but a fixed cycle fits few foods, and a mat inside a microwave cavity is awkward.

title: I33 Pull-to-Cook Handle
new_elements: I33 Pull-to-cook handle (Pulling the handle winds a simple timer and latches, while pushing it stops early)
rationale: Pull and push are universal gestures that replace a separate start and stop mechanism.
judge_comment: A pull-and-push handle is a concrete mechanical timer that is easy to grasp, but it conflicts with how doors normally open and needs redesign.

title: I34 Glowing Choke-Seal Countdown
new_elements: I34 Glowing choke-seal countdown (The door seal lights progressively as time passes, combining sealing and visible countdown)
rationale: Time is visible where the user already looks, so no separate dial or bell must be interpreted.
judge_comment: A progressive light on the seal is an elegant countdown, but it does not simplify start or setup, and lighting a choke seal is technically odd.

title: I35 Steam-Stop Auto Cook
new_elements: I35 Steam-stop auto cook (A simple steam sensor ends the cycle when food begins boiling, replacing manual timing)
rationale: Food state decides when to stop, so the user never needs to choose a time.
judge_comment: Steam sensing to end the cycle already exists in sensor-cook microwaves and removes the time choice, though it only suits foods that steam.

title: I36 Single More Button
new_elements: I36 Single more button (One button starts a short cycle and every extra press adds a fixed amount of safe energy)
rationale: A single more button collapses two controls into one action and is instantly understandable.
judge_comment: One button with incremental presses is very simple and already close to existing 'add 30 seconds' buttons, though it is a clear substitution for the usual controls.

title: I37 Door-Only Stop Control
new_elements: I37 Door-only stop control (Opening the door is the only stop control, with no buttons to press or settings to reset)
rationale: The intuitive way to interrupt, opening the door, becomes the only thing the user must know.
judge_comment: Door opening already pauses microwaves, so this is intuitive and feasible but barely new.

title: I38 Self-Resetting Timer
new_elements: I38 Self-resetting timer (The timer automatically returns to zero at the end so the next user sees a clear ready state)
rationale: A zero state tells every new user the appliance is ready without explanation.
judge_comment: Auto-reset to zero helps show a ready state, but it is a minor tweak and already common.

title: I39 Color Heat Ring
new_elements: I39 Color heat ring (A glowing ring shifts from blue to red to indicate average heating power without numbers)
rationale: Color intensity is easier to understand than power steps or percentages.
judge_comment: A color ring is an intuitive power indicator, but it adds an element and does not simplify operation much, since power choice still exists.

title: I40 Case-Flash End Alert
new_elements: I40 Case-flash end alert (The whole door flashes at the end of cooking, replacing both the lamp and the bell)
rationale: A flashing surface is an unmistakable ready signal that needs no listening or dial reading.
judge_comment: A flashing door is an unmistakable cue, but it is weaker on operation simplicity and is awkward to implement on a shielded door.

title: I41 Door Edge Pull Release
new_elements: I41 Door edge pull release (A soft edge lip lets the door be pulled open directly, removing the need for a release button)
rationale: Pulling the door edge is a natural action, so no separate button must be discovered.
judge_comment: Pull-open door is intuitive and already common in some microwaves, so it helps simplicity but is not very radical.

title: I42 Timer-Cam Turntable
new_elements: I42 Timer-cam turntable (The turntable is driven by the mechanical timer cam instead of a separate motor)
rationale: Fewer moving parts mean fewer surprising stalls or noises that confuse users.
judge_comment: A cam-driven turntable is a concrete cost-saving substitution, but it barely affects how users operate the microwave.

title: I43 Bare-Cabinet Preset Slot
new_elements: I43 Bare-cabinet preset slot (The fascia disappears and a simple slot accepts a key to set time)
rationale: A single obvious slot removes visual clutter and the need to interpret panel controls.
judge_comment: A key slot is radical, but needing a key to set time adds a new learning step and may be less intuitive.

title: I44 One-Magnet Door Cut
new_elements: I44 One-magnet door cut (A simple magnet switch replaces complex door interlock logic so users feel only the natural door action)
rationale: The user only interacts with the door, and the safety cutout becomes invisible rather than confusing.
judge_comment: A magnet door switch is feasible and makes safety invisible, but it is largely an internal change and is already standard practice.

title: I45 Lamp Glow Timer
new_elements: I45 Lamp glow timer (The interior lamp brightens then fades to show remaining time, replacing the timer dial)
rationale: Light level acts as a universal timer, so no numbers or settings are needed.
judge_comment: Using lamp brightness as a timer is highly novel and number-free, but it is ambiguous for setting time and imprecise.

title: I46 Sunlight Guide Inside
new_elements: I46 Sunlight guide inside (A fiber optic tube brings ambient light into the cavity, eliminating a bulb)
rationale: Passive daylight makes viewing simple and removes a component that can fail or need replacing.
judge_comment: Fiber-optic daylight is unreliable in a kitchen and barely affects operation simplicity; an LED bulb is already cheap and long-lived.

title: I47 RF-Blocking Glass Door
new_elements: I47 RF-blocking glass door (A solid transparent microwave-reflective glass replaces the perforated window and light bulb)
rationale: A normal-looking clear door is instantly understandable and needs no explanation of mesh or lighting.
judge_comment: A transparent RF-reflective door is plausible with conductive coatings, but it only slightly helps ease of use, and removing the light leaves the interior dark.

title: I48 Cup-Mat Heating Trigger
new_elements: I48 Cup-mat heating trigger (A shaped mug mat starts a beverage cycle when a cup is placed on it)
rationale: A familiar mug shape becomes the setting, so there is nothing to program.
judge_comment: Placing a cup to auto-start a beverage cycle is intuitive, but detection and safety, such as an empty or wrong-sized cup, are challenging.

title: I49 One-Slot Power Plate
new_elements: I49 One-slot power plate (A sliding plate with two obvious detents replaces the five-step power knob)
rationale: Two clear stops are easier than reading a multi-position dial, especially at first use.
judge_comment: A two-detent slider is simple and mechanically feasible, though it limits power control and is only an incremental simplification.

title: I50 Full-Face Touch Plate
new_elements: I50 Full-face touch plate (The entire front panel starts a default heating cycle when pressed anywhere)
rationale: Any touch works, so the user never needs to locate or understand controls.
judge_comment: Whole-panel touch needs no learning, but accidental starts and one default cycle fit few foods, and no time control is provided.

title: 1. One-Press Start Pad
new_elements: Single-press start pad (Replaces timer and power knobs with a pressure pad on the door or fascia.); One-touch default heating (Press to start a simple default cook, hold to extend, release to stop.)
judge_comment: A single press-to-start pad is highly simple and workable, but it is close to existing start buttons and the default cook may suit few foods.

title: 2. QR Code Meal Trigger
new_elements: QR cooking trigger (A simple scanner or camera pad replaces knob programming with one scan.); Scan-to-cook preset (The food package tells the microwave what to do without user settings.)
judge_comment: Scan-to-cook removes settings entirely and is fairly novel, but it depends on packaging adoption and a connected database, and it needs a fallback for food without a code.

title: 3. Color Ring Door Feedback
new_elements: Color-ring door indicator (An outer light ring replaces lamp and bell functions with a single color state.); Visible ready signal (Green, amber, and red tell the user whether to start, wait, or remove food.)
judge_comment: Color states are intuitive and cheap, but they only give feedback and do not simplify operation, and similar indicators already exist.

title: 4. Transparent Cavity Door
new_elements: Transparent RF-safe door (A shielded transparent panel replaces perforated mesh and interior lamp.); See food without lamp (The user watches cooking directly through the door with no light or holes needed.)
judge_comment: A transparent RF-safe door is an interesting substitution, but it does little for ease of operation and shielding without a mesh is hard.

title: 5. Thermochromic Finish Indicator
new_elements: Thermochromic finish film (A heat-sensitive surface inside the cavity changes color when done.); Food done by color (Color change replaces the bell as a natural, no-learning feedback signal.)
judge_comment: Color change as a doneness cue is intuitive and novel, but a film in the cavity is impractical because it is non-reversible, gets dirty, and does not measure the food's state.

title: 6. Magnetic Door Interlock
new_elements: Magnetic door interlock (Replaces switches, lever, and button with magnetically encoded door closure.); Door-close powers safely (The door itself tells the appliance whether heating may continue.)
judge_comment: Door-closure-as-start is simple, but microwaves already use interlocks and it does little to remove the learning curve.

title: 7. Weight-Set Timer
new_elements: Weight sensing turntable (The tray measures load and sets a default time without any knobs.); Weight-based default time (Heavy items get longer heating, light items get shorter heating automatically.)
judge_comment: Weight-based auto time removes the need to set a timer, though weight correlates imperfectly with the heating needed.

title: 8. Inside-Camera Visibility
new_elements: RF-hardened cavity camera (A shielded camera replaces the mesh window and lamp viewing function.); External food view (The user sees food on a phone or display without opening the door.)
judge_comment: A camera aids visibility but adds complexity and does not simplify operation; it also duplicates the existing window.

title: 9. Aroma End Signal
new_elements: Heat-triggered scent capsule (A safe scent capsule activates when the food is ready.); Smell signals done (The user recognizes readiness by smell instead of learning sounds or displays.)
judge_comment: A scent signal needs no learning and is wild, but single-use capsules, heat-triggering and food-safety concerns make it impractical.

title: 10. Touchless Door Release
new_elements: Capacitive door release (Replaces the mechanical push button with a no-press proximity release.); Touchless open (The door opens when hands approach, removing a small mechanical interaction.)
judge_comment: A touchless release is easy to use but risks accidental opening and gives a marginal simplification.

title: 11. Passive Field-Shaping Tray
new_elements: Passive RF-shaped tray (A shaped reflective mat replaces turntable, motor, and roller ring functions.); Even heat without rotation (The tray sculpts the field so food does not need a moving turntable.)
judge_comment: A passive RF-shaping mat could replace the turntable, but it doesn't simplify operation for the user and static field shaping is hard to make even.

title: 12. Smart Color Food Sticker
new_elements: Cooking color sticker (A food-safe microwave-transparent sticker changes behavior based on heat.); Color tells time not knob (The sticker or user follows a simple color rule instead of setting a timer.)
judge_comment: A color-change indicator removes the need to set a timer and is intuitive, but the microwave can't read the sticker and the mechanism is vague.

title: 13. Door Handle Duration Dial
new_elements: Door handle dial (The door handle becomes the only control for opening and setting time.); Handle sets duration (Turn or pull the same handle to open the door or choose the default heat.)
judge_comment: Merging door opening and time setting into one handle is simple and plausible, but a default duration limits flexibility.

title: 14. Vibrating Door Ding
new_elements: Piezo door vibrator (Replaces the mechanical bell with a door-integrated vibration signal.); Door shakes when done (The door itself becomes the ready signal wherever the user is.)
judge_comment: A piezo door vibration signal is feasible and concrete but only marginally helps ease of operation, and it may not be noticed.

title: 15. Pressure-Container Start
new_elements: Pressure pad container start (A pad on the food container starts the microwave when squeezed.); Squeeze container to heat (The action that gets the food also starts cooking, with no knobs.)
judge_comment: A squeeze-to-start container is radical and needs no learning, but it requires a wireless link and special containers, which makes it impractical.

title: 16. Glow-Coat Cavity
new_elements: Phosphorescent cavity coat (A light-absorbing cavity surface glows instead of using an interior bulb.); Ambient cavity view (The user can glance inside without a separate lamp or button.)
judge_comment: A glowing cavity coat barely affects operation simplicity, and phosphorescence fades and would be dim.

title: 17. Magnetic Puck Start
new_elements: Magnetic start puck (A single removable puck attaches to the door to start heating.); Puck starts simple heat (One magnetic action starts a default cycle, replacing all knobs and buttons.)
judge_comment: A single magnetic puck to start a default cycle is very simple, though it can be lost and offers little control.

title: 18. Infrared Auto Stop
new_elements: Infrared food sensor (A small IR eye inside the cavity measures surface temperature.); Auto stop at target (The microwave stops itself when food reaches a safe target temperature.)
judge_comment: IR auto-stop removes the need to set time or power, directly eliminating the learning curve, though surface sensing is imperfect and the sensor must be protected from microwaves.

title: 19. Light-Pipe Illumination
new_elements: Microwave light pipe (External room light is channeled into the cavity through a dielectric pipe.); No bulb cavity view (The user sees inside without any replaceable interior lamp.)
judge_comment: A light pipe into the cavity is a clever but impractical substitution that risks microwave leakage and does little for ease of use.

title: 20. Mug-Fixing Cavity
new_elements: Fixed mug shelf cavity (A shelf holds common mugs in place and removes the turntable motor.); Drinks heat without turning (The user simply places a mug and starts a fixed drink cycle.)
judge_comment: A fixed-mug shelf with a single drink cycle is simple but limited in use and heats unevenly without a turntable.

title: 21. Thermochromic Wrap Timer
new_elements: Color-changing food wrap (A microwave-safe wrap changes color as the food reaches readiness.); Wrap glows when done (The wrap becomes the timer and end signal without user programming.)
judge_comment: A thermochromic wrap that signals doneness is radical and removes timer programming, but it is hard to calibrate across foods and doesn't actually control the oven.

title: 22. Infinite Up-Only Knob
new_elements: Endless start knob (Replaces two knobs with one infinite clockwise-only knob.); Turn up to add time (Only one direction means the user cannot get lost in negative settings.)
judge_comment: A single endless clockwise knob is simple, cheap and easily built, though it is a modest tweak on existing dials.

title: 23. Whole-Front Touch Control
new_elements: Capacitive front panel (The entire front becomes a touch surface with one heat zone.); Tap to heat (Tap any part of the panel to start or stop the simple cooking mode.)
judge_comment: A single tap-anywhere touch surface with one heat mode is simple to use but offers little control and risks accidental activation.

title: 24. Door-Autostop Seal
new_elements: Magnetic interlock seal (The door seal itself cuts power when separation is detected.); Open door cancels RF (The appliance resets by opening the door, no stop button needed.)
judge_comment: Interlocks already cut power when the door opens, so this is a minor change and does little for learning-curve reduction.

title: 25. Waveform Stirrer
new_elements: RF waveform stirrer (A solid-state pattern source replaces moving food through the field.); Moves pattern not food (The heat pattern rotates instead of the plate, making use simpler.)
judge_comment: A solid-state RF source with a rotating pattern is a technically interesting substitute for the turntable, but its link to user simplicity is weak and it is costly.

title: 26. Self-Returning Start Knob
new_elements: Spring-return start knob (A knob returns to zero and sets time by how long it is pushed.); Push-time by dwell (The longer you hold, the longer it heats, without reading a dial.)
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat spring knob is intuitive and cheap, though it is hard to set long times precisely and holding is tiring.

title: 27. Haptic Clickless Button
new_elements: Silent haptic button (Replaces mechanical button action with a single silent haptic touch.); Press feedback without noise (The user feels start and stop states without learning mechanical positions.)
judge_comment: A haptic button is feasible but adds little to ease of use and may be less intuitive than a physical button.

title: 28. Visible Timer via Door Edge
new_elements: Door-edge LED strip (Replaces lamp, bell, and dial state with one glowing door edge.); Time left shown by color (The edge shifts from cool to warm as the cycle completes.)
judge_comment: A glowing door edge gives easy glanceable status and is cheap, but it doesn't help with input, and color alone may be ambiguous.

title: 29. Voice-Only Default
new_elements: One-word voice trigger (A local voice trigger replaces all knobs with one simple command.); Say heat to start (The user says heat, and the appliance starts the simplest default cycle.)
judge_comment: A single-word voice command has almost no learning curve, but one default cycle limits usefulness and noisy kitchens hurt reliability.

title: 30. Camera Ready Ping
new_elements: Cooking status camera AI (A camera plus local classifier replaces lamp and bell with visual done detection.); Ready ping to user (The appliance signals done when the food visually appears ready.)
judge_comment: Visual doneness detection is radical and removes timing decisions, but it is costly and unreliable across foods and does not simplify starting.

title: 31. Color-Shift Power Puck
new_elements: Color-coded power puck (A small puck replaces the 5-step power knob with a color slot.); Puck sets simple power (One puck color selects the best default for most users.)
judge_comment: A color puck replacing the power knob is simple and plausible, but it adds a loose part and only removes one control.

title: 32. Tactile Universal Dial
new_elements: Raised tactile dial (A single raised dial with bumps replaces both knobs and the flat fascia.); One dial by feel (The user can set cooking by touch without looking or reading labels.)
judge_comment: A single tactile dial is highly feasible and intuitive, but it is an incremental simplification rather than a radical one.

title: 33. Food-Surface IR Stop
new_elements: Surface IR stop sensor (A sensor aimed at the food surface stops heating when hot.); Stops when surface safe (No time guess is needed because the food surface controls the stop.)
judge_comment: Surface-temperature stopping removes time guessing, which fits zero learning curve, though IR only reads the surface and can misjudge food heated unevenly inside.

title: 34. Scent Diffuser Timer
new_elements: Micro scent diffuser (A tiny timed scent release replaces the bell as the end signal.); Scent marks end (The user recognizes the cooking end from a simple pleasant smell.)
judge_comment: A scent end signal is novel, but it is unreliable, can be unpleasant or allergenic, and does not simplify operation.

title: 35. Static Turntable Mat
new_elements: Static RF scattering mat (A fixed mat with patterned features replaces the rotating tray system.); Even heating without turn (Food does not need to move because the field is shaped at the plate.)
judge_comment: A static RF scattering mat is bold, but evenly shaped fields are hard to achieve, and it has little effect on operating simplicity.

title: 36. Magnetron-Free Solid-State Source
new_elements: Solid-state microwave amplifier (A digital source replaces the magnetron and high-voltage chain.); Digital continuous heat (The user gets simple fixed heat modes because the source is controllable by code, not knobs.)
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is real and enables simple fixed modes, but the link to zero learning curve is indirect and the cost is high.

title: 37. Conductive Mesh Invisible Window
new_elements: Transparent conductive mesh door (A nearly invisible shielded film replaces coarse door holes and bulb.); See food without lamp (The user can watch food clearly without needing the door light to turn on.)
judge_comment: Mesh doors already exist; visibility helps a little but does little for operation simplicity.

title: 38. Bell-Free LED Pulse
new_elements: Pulsing LED door ring (Replaces the mechanical bell with a visual pulse on the door ring.); Light pulse done signal (A slow blink tells the user when to remove food, without a sound to learn.)
judge_comment: A visual done-signal is easy and intuitive, though a silent slow blink may be missed and the idea is not radical.

title: 39. Magnetic Latch Only
new_elements: Magnetic latch door (A simple magnetic latch replaces button, lever, and multiple interlock switches.); Close starts and holds (Closing the door starts and maintains the safest default state.)
judge_comment: Close-to-start is very simple to use, but it risks accidental starts, and safety regulations require redundant interlocks.

title: 40. Door-Open Auto Cancel
new_elements: Door-open reset switch (A single switch detects door separation and returns the control to zero.); Opening cancels timer (The user never needs a stop button because opening the door stops everything.)
judge_comment: Opening the door to cancel is already standard behavior, but it is intuitive and removes the need for a stop button.

title: 41. Smart Tray RFID
new_elements: RFID meal tray (A tray tag tells the microwave the default mode, removing knob settings.); Tray programs appliance (The user just places the tagged tray and closes the door.)
judge_comment: RFID-tagged trays could remove settings entirely, plausible with existing tech, but it requires proprietary trays and the substitution is more of an add-on.

title: 42. One-Twist Time Ring
new_elements: Around-door time ring (A ring around the door replaces the timer knob with a large intuitive arc.); Twist ring to set heat (The user moves the ring to a colored heat zone, not minutes.)
judge_comment: A door ring with color heat zones is intuitive and simple to build, though it is only a modest departure from a knob.

title: 43. Heat-Activated Squeeze Bell
new_elements: Thermal bell striker (Heat expansion releases a bell hammer instead of a timer cam.); Heat triggers bell (The bell sounds only when the food is hot, so no timing skill is needed.)
judge_comment: A heat-triggered bell is a creative mechanical substitution, but heating food in a microwave and sensing its temperature this way is hard, and it does not control the cooking itself.

title: 44. Auto Power by Weight
new_elements: Weight-based power switch (A load sensor chooses the safest default power from food mass.); Weight sets power (The user does not learn power levels because the tray selects them.)
judge_comment: Load-cell power selection is feasible and cuts the decisions the user has to make, but weight alone is a poor proxy for the right power or time.

title: 45. Glow in Dark End
new_elements: Glow end indicator (A glow-in-the-dark strip lights up when the cycle ends.); Cavity glows when done (No sound or dial reading is needed because the glow is obvious.)
judge_comment: A glow strip only signals that the cycle is done, which does little for operation; phosphorescence also isn't truly a trigger-on-completion indicator.

title: 46. Phone App Single Button
new_elements: Phone start button (A smartphone interface replaces appliance knobs with one big Heat button.); One tap from phone (The appliance itself stays visually simple because control moves to the phone.)
judge_comment: A phone app adds a step and dependency, so it is arguably harder than a button, and smart microwaves with apps already exist.

title: 47. Door Handle Start Lever
new_elements: Start lever handle (The door lever becomes both opener and timer by movement length.); Close and pull to start (One handle gesture replaces learning two separate controls.)
judge_comment: A lever that opens, closes and sets the timer by movement is intuitive and merges two controls, though the timing precision is unclear.

title: 48. Color-Blocking Safety Lock
new_elements: Red-green safety lock (A color-coded door lock shows whether heating is possible.); Color says safe (The user sees green to go, red to stop, with no instruction manual.)
judge_comment: A color-coded lock gives a clear status cue, but it addresses safety more than operation and is only a modest substitution.

title: 49. Transparent Front without Lamp
new_elements: Full transparent RF casing (The whole visible front becomes microwave-shielded transparent material.); Cavity visible no light (The user never needs to open the door or turn on an interior lamp.)
judge_comment: A fully transparent shielded front removes the lamp and door-opening checks, but it is costly and only loosely tied to ease of operation.

title: 50. Self-Clearing Start Timer
new_elements: Auto-return start button (A button physically resets after the cycle, replacing knob readback.); Button clears after end (The user always sees a neutral start position, so there is nothing to remember.)
judge_comment: A start button that physically resets leaves a neutral state and is simple and feasible, but the gain in ease of use is small.

title: Drop-in Time Capsule
new_elements: Gravity-dropped capsule timer (Starts the microwave when a physical time capsule falls into a slot.); Timer slot with physical time capsules (One capsule per common duration; dropping it sets and starts the oven.)
rationale: One physical drop replaces dial reading and setting, making timing instantly understandable.
judge_comment: A physical capsule that sets and starts the oven is a radical, intuitive no-learning-curve interface, though capsule management and flexibility are concerns.

title: Squeeze-to-Start Lever
new_elements: Single-lever duration and power actuation (A squeeze lever simultaneously selects time and power by mechanical stop depth.); Squeeze-to-start lever (A large handle squeezed once starts cooking with preset duration and power.)
rationale: A single squeeze replaces two knobs with one obvious gesture.
judge_comment: A single squeeze gesture is simple, but mapping both time and power to stop depth is ambiguous and imprecise.

title: Color Power Plate
new_elements: Color-coded mechanical power stop (One colored plate position maps directly to a fixed heating level.); Single color power plate (A sliding plate with one intuitive color selection for power level.)
rationale: One color choice removes numeric power dial interpretation.
judge_comment: Color-coded power selection is easy to build and understand, but it only addresses power and is not very radical.

title: Pull-Tab Door Release
new_elements: Pull-open release lever (A fabric tab pulls the latch open without pressing a small button.); Fabric pull-tab latch (A soft pull tab on the door edge opens the cavity by natural pulling motion.)
rationale: Pulling a tab is more obvious than pressing a hidden latch button.
judge_comment: A pull tab is plausible and intuitive but only affects door opening, which is marginal to learning operation.

title: Transparent Glass Door
new_elements: Fused conductive transparent shielding (Microscopic conductive strands in glass block RF while staying visible.); Microwave-safe transparent glass door (A see-through door that needs no perforated mesh and no extra interior light.)
rationale: Direct visibility removes the guesswork of checking food during cooking.
judge_comment: A transparent door helps monitoring but does little for operation simplicity, and the RF shielding claim is questionable.

title: Door-Open Duration Timer
new_elements: Door-angle mechanical duration mapping (The time a door is held open sets the next countdown by a spring cam.); Door-open duration timer (Users time cooking by how long they leave the door open before closing.)
rationale: It merges opening the door with setting the time, reducing separate steps.
judge_comment: Novel but unintuitive; users must learn that door-open time sets cooking time, which works against a no-learning-curve goal.

title: Load-Weight Start Mat
new_elements: Spring-balance automatic timer and power selection (Food weight moves a spring scale to set both time and power mechanically.); Load-weight start mat (A floor mat inside the cavity that starts the microwave when food is placed.)
rationale: Simply putting food on the plate removes all manual controls.
judge_comment: Placing food to auto-start is very intuitive, but a mechanical spring scale cannot reliably infer the right time and power, and starting without the door closed is a safety issue.

title: Combined Time-Power Dial
new_elements: Dual-cam single-knob selector (One knob moves both a time cam and a power cam to matching settings.); Combined time-power dial (A single large dial chooses ready-to-use combinations of time and power.)
rationale: One dial replaces two knobs and prevents mismatched time and power choices.
judge_comment: A single dial of combined presets is simple and highly feasible, but it is an incremental idea.

title: Icon-Only Door Plate
new_elements: Pictogram preset cam bank (Door icons map to fixed mechanical time and power combinations.); Icon-only preset door plate (Pressing a food icon on the door selects the whole operation.)
rationale: Recognizable icons let users choose a meal without reading numbers.
judge_comment: Pictogram presets avoid reading numbers and are easy to build, but they are common and limited in flexibility.

title: Magnetic Countdown Puck
new_elements: Magnetic snap-on timer (A puck attached to the door sets countdown by magnet position on a scale.); Magnetic countdown puck (A removable puck users place on the door to select duration.)
rationale: Placing a magnetic puck is more tactile and obvious than turning a knob.
judge_comment: A tactile magnetic puck is a bit playful, but it is a hard-to-interpret scale on the door and adds a loose part that can be lost.

title: Condensation End Indicator
new_elements: Evaporation-driven start duration (Water condensation on a cold indicator sets a mechanical countdown as it clears.); Condensation end indicator (A small visible element that returns to normal when cooking should end.)
rationale: Users can rely on a physical end signal instead of calculating time.
judge_comment: A condensation-based end cue is creative, but it is unreliable across foods and humidity, and it does not set a start duration in any practical way.

title: Clap-Start Piezo Switch
new_elements: Acoustic piezo start trigger (A piezo sensor converts one sharp clap into a fixed start pulse.); Clap-start piezo switch (A small sensor panel that starts a preset cycle when it hears a clap.)
rationale: One obvious sound gesture can start a default cooking cycle.
judge_comment: Clap-start is easy to build and simple to use, but it risks false triggers from ambient noise and a fixed preset limits control.

title: Shape-Memory Handle Retractor
new_elements: Thermal shape-memory end signal (A shape-memory wire moves a handle when the timer completes.); Shape-memory handle retractor (The door handle shifts visibly at the end of cooking.)
rationale: A physical handle movement is easier to notice than a bell or beep.
judge_comment: A shape-memory wire moving the handle is a tangible, concrete end signal, though it only covers the end of the cycle and the wire needs resetting and cooling.

title: Color-Coded Cup Tray
new_elements: Tray-thickness power attenuation (Different colored tray bases mechanically limit heating intensity.); Color-coded cup tray (The tray placed under the cup sets power by its color and thickness.)
rationale: Picking a colored tray is simpler than remembering power numbers.
judge_comment: Setting power by tray color is intuitive, but a tray cannot attenuate microwave heating in a controlled way, so it is technically dubious.

title: Close-to-Start Interlock
new_elements: Door-close latch timing (Fully closing the door directly activates a default cooking cycle.); Close-to-start interlock (The door latch starts the microwave as soon as it closes.)
rationale: Closing the door becomes the only action needed to start cooking.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start is highly intuitive and easy to build, but it is a safety concern and accidental starts are a risk, and the idea is not very radical.

title: Pull-Open Launch Latch
new_elements: Pull-force mechanical timer (Pulling the door against a spring sets duration by pull distance.); Pull-open launch latch (A latch where a firm pull both opens access and starts a short preset time.)
rationale: One door pull combines opening and starting, reducing steps.
judge_comment: Opening and starting in one pull is simple, but starting a cycle on opening is a safety problem and a fixed preset limits use.

title: Turntable Start Switch
new_elements: Rotating floor trigger timer (A quarter turn of the rotating plate engages a start cam.); Turntable start switch (A simple rotation of the plate starts a default cycle.)
rationale: Rotating the plate is an intuitive motion that eliminates separate start controls.
judge_comment: Turning the plate to start is intuitive in theory, but the plate sits inside the cavity, which makes it awkward and unsafe to reach and operate.

title: Spring-Tension Door Timer
new_elements: Door torsion spring duration (Winding the door handle against a torsion spring stores and releases time.); Spring-tension door timer (Twisting the door handle sets the countdown without a separate dial.)
rationale: It puts timing into the door handle, where users already reach to interact.
judge_comment: A wind-up handle timer is familiar and needs no learning, and it is plausible mechanically, though it must be integrated with the door interlocks.

title: Fixed Mug Cavity Insert
new_elements: Mug-shaped RF confinement (A molded insert focuses heating for one common object and locks the cycle.); Fixed mug cavity insert (A built-in mug holder that starts cooking when the mug is seated and door closed.)
rationale: A dedicated mug slot makes a one-action routine possible.
judge_comment: A dedicated mug slot gives true one-action use, but it is single-purpose, and an RF confinement insert is questionable physically.

title: Melting Time Capsule Timer
new_elements: Phase-change mechanical timer (A sealed capsule melts at a calibrated rate to drive a switch back.); Melting time capsule timer (A warm cavity capsule physically changes position to mark duration.)
rationale: A visible melting capsule gives users a natural countdown without numbers.
judge_comment: A melting-capsule timer is very novel, but it is imprecise, not reusable, and a poor fit for simple operation.

title: Reversible Temperature Strip
new_elements: Color-changing thermal end indicator (A thermal strip changes color at target temperature and resets by cooling.); Reversible temperature strip (A door-mounted strip that turns green or red to indicate heating state.)
rationale: Color change replaces mental cooking calculations with a clear signal.
judge_comment: A temperature strip gives a clear signal, but it shows only the end state, not the operation, and a door-mounted strip would struggle in a microwave environment.

title: Vibrating Handle End Indicator
new_elements: Cam-driven vibration end indicator (A timer cam releases an eccentric weight that shakes the handle.); Vibrating handle (The door handle vibrates gently when cooking finishes.)
rationale: Vibration near the hand is more likely to be noticed than a distant bell.
judge_comment: A cam-released eccentric weight in the handle is a concrete and plausible mechanical substitute for a bell, though it only affects the end alert rather than overall operation.

title: Tinted Glass Countdown Door
new_elements: Mechanical tinted glass rotation (A rotating tinted panel darkens or clears as a time dial advances.); Tinted glass countdown door (The door window visually fades to show remaining cooking time.)
rationale: Seeing time fade through the door makes remaining duration intuitive.
judge_comment: A fading door shows remaining time intuitively, but a mechanically rotating tinted panel is awkward, and it must not compromise the door's shielding.

title: Inductive Tap Power Switch
new_elements: Magnetron coil tap (A mechanical selector changes inductive coupling instead of cycling on and off.); Inductive tap power switch (One slide switch gives gentler heating without complex electronics.)
rationale: A single slide replaces confusing power numbers and improves gentle heating clarity.
judge_comment: A single slide switch for power would be simple, but 'inductive coupling taps' on a magnetron is technically dubious and vague.

title: Dial-as-Tray
new_elements: Rotating tray cam timer (Turning the interior tray itself selects time and power through hidden cams.); Dial-as-tray (The food plate rotates to positions that set the cycle mechanically.)
rationale: Adjusting the plate users already touch is simpler than manipulating knobs.
judge_comment: Setting the cycle by turning the tray is radical and intuitive in concept, but the cam linkage inside the cavity is impractical and hard to keep clean.

title: Lift-Cup Start Switch
new_elements: Container lift mechanical trigger (Lifting a cup after a heating cycle releases a mechanical latch or start cam.); Lift-cup start switch (A spring-loaded cup rest that starts when lifted and returns when replaced.)
rationale: It uses the natural lift action for starting and stopping, not extra controls.
judge_comment: Lift-to-start is intuitive, but starting heating on lift is odd and unsafe-sounding, and the stop/start logic is confusing.

title: Single Rubber Operation Button
new_elements: Multi-pose mechanical button (One large rubber button switches modes based on press depth.); Single rubber operation button (A soft big button users can press gently, normally, or deeply for presets.)
rationale: One obvious button replaces multiple controls with depth-based presets.
judge_comment: One big button is simple, but depth-based presets need discovery and may not be obvious without learning.

title: Loop-Rope Door Pull
new_elements: Rope-and-pulley release (A looped rope transmits a pull from a large handle to the latch.); Loop-rope door pull (A soft loop the user pulls anywhere to open the door.)
rationale: A large rope loop is easier to locate and grasp than a small button.
judge_comment: A rope pull is easy to find, but it is not obviously simpler than a handle and does not address operation settings.

title: Open-Top Shielded Basket
